procedural_history.originating_court: Sessions Court (Trial Court) - heard Sessions Trials No. 160 of 30.07.2012, 275 of 04.12.2012 and 114 of 15.04.2013
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 11.02.2016 and order dated 17.02.2016 in Criminal Appeal bearing No. 249 DB of 2016
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 249 DB of 2016 and issued a judgment on 11.02.2016 and an order on 17.02.2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard Criminal Appeal No(s). 1378-1379 of 2023 and partly allowed the appeals.

directions: The sentence of Raju, Parveen, Sunder s/o Amit Lal, Sandeep, Nar Singh, and Sunder s/o Rajpal is hereby modified; they are hereby sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment for five years.
They shall surrender and serve the rest of their sentences within six weeks from today.

issue.issue_text: Appropriateness of the sentences imposed on the appellants.

facts: The High Court convicted eight accused persons for the same offense (culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC).
Instead of imposing a uniform sentence, the High Court sentenced each accused to the period of imprisonment they had already undergone.
This resulted in a wide and unexplained disparity in sentences, ranging from 11 months for one accused to over 9 years for another.
The High Court had not identified any distinguishing features or separate roles played by each accused that would justify such different sentences.
law: The principle of proportionality should guide the sentencing process.
Sentencing must take into account the gravity of the offense, the nature of the crime, and the manner in which it was committed.
When all accused are held equally liable for an offense without distinct roles, imposing widely disparate sentences without a clear rationale is flawed.
Mechanically applying a "sentence undergone" criteria can be an aberration and lead to a failure of justice if it results in grossly inadequate sentences.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's sentencing to be "inexplicable (if not downright bizarre)" due to the wide disparity without any supporting rationale.
The Court noted that the High Court's reasoning was inconsistent; for example, if age were a factor, the 61-year-old accused (A-1) would not have received one of the stiffest sentences.

The primary error of the High Court was its failure to consider the gravity of the offense. Having found all accused equally guilty, it was an "aberration" to then impose such varied and, for some, inadequate sentences.
The Court concluded that the imposition of the "sentence undergone" criteria in this specific case was flawed because it ignored the seriousness of the crime and the principle of proportionality.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found the sentences inappropriate. It held that the High Court erred by applying a "sentence undergone" standard, which created an inexplicable and flawed disparity. The Court ruled that, given the gravity of the offense and the equal liability of the accused, a uniform sentence of five years' rigorous imprisonment was appropriate. It modified the sentences for those who had served less than five years, while leaving the sentences of two accused who had already served more than that period undisturbed.

arguments.issue_text: Appropriateness of the sentences imposed on the appellants.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that the High Court's judgment was gravely flawed in adopting the 'sentence undergone' as the standard for sentencing.

This approach resulted in widely different and disparate sentences for the accused, who were all convicted for the same offense (under Section 304 Part II r/w Section 149 IPC) without any distinguishing roles being identified for each individual.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's sentencing was appropriate as it followed salutary principles by considering mitigating factors such as the relative ages of the accused, their family circumstances, the length of time they had already spent in custody, and the time that had elapsed since the crime was committed.

cases.case_name: Jameel v. State of U. P.
cases.principle: Sentencing should be a fact-dependent exercise where the law adopts corrective machinery or deterrence based on the factual matrix. The process should be stern where required and tempered with mercy where warranted, considering all circumstances of the crime, including its nature, planning, commission, motive, the accused's conduct, and weapons used.
The provided text does not specify the legal principle for which this case was cited, only that it was 'relied on'.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When multiple accused are held equally and vicariously liable for the same offense, and there are no distinguishing features in their individual roles, the imposition of a 'sentence undergone' standard that results in wide and unexplained disparities in punishment is an aberration and constitutes a flawed sentencing process.
obiter: The principle of proportionality should guide the sentencing process.
Imposing meagre sentences merely on account of the lapse of time is counterproductive.

Sentencing should be a fact-dependent exercise, considering the nature of the crime, the manner in which it was planned and committed, the motive, the conduct of the accused, the nature of weapons used, and all other attending circumstances.
The law should adopt corrective machinery or deterrence based on the factual matrix, with sentencing being stern where it should be and tempered with mercy where it is warranted.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Having held all the accused criminally liable, u/s. 304 Part II r/w s.149 IPC and also not having found any distinguishing feature in the form of separate roles played by each of them, the imposition of the “sentence undergone” criteria, amounted to aberration, and the sentencing is for that reason, flawed. The High Court's sentencing was inexplicable as no rationale appeared from its reasoning for the wide disparity in sentences for the same offence, and it fell into error by not considering the gravity of the offence.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of proportionality should guide the sentencing process.

Sentencing should be a fact-dependent exercise where the law adopts corrective machinery or deterrence based on the factual matrix, including the nature of the crime, the manner it was committed, motive, conduct of the accused, and weapons used.
It is the duty of the court to see that an appropriate and adequate sentence is imposed, having regard to the commission of the crime and its impact on the social order.
Punishment is designed to protect society by deterring potential offenders, preventing the guilty party from repeating the offence, and reforming the offender.
why_appellant_lost: The appeal was only partly allowed; for the two accused (A-1 and A-6) who had already served more than the newly imposed five-year sentence, the court left the High Court's judgment undisturbed as a practical matter.
why_respondent_won: While the respondent's defense of the High Court's reasoning was rejected, they succeeded in ensuring that a substantial and uniform sentence of five years rigorous imprisonment was imposed on the appellants who had served less time, thereby preventing them from being released on the basis of the flawed 'sentence undergone' standard.
policy_considerations: Imposing meagre sentences merely on account of lapse of time is counterproductive.

The imposition of the “sentence undergone” criteria, when it results in wide and inexplicable disparity for accused persons convicted for the same offense with no distinguishing roles, amounts to an aberration in the sentencing process.
The sentencing process should be stern where it should be, and tempered with mercy where it warrants to be, through a deft modulation based on the facts of the case.
